decisions.when: Best when verified after-tax net proceeds exceed risk-adjusted hold value, remaining term is short, buyer pricing is executable, or concentration/liquidity risk is unacceptable.
decisions.tradeoffs: crystallizes value and reduces single-tenant/hazard exposure; may trigger tax, transfer costs, and loss of future upside.
decisions.required: Executed lease, obligor/guaranty, rent roll, title, debt payoff, tax basis, appraisal/BOV, insurance, and closing-cost estimate.
decisions.verdict: Prepare now; do not commit without verified net proceeds and hold comparison.

decisions.when: Best when the actual obligor is creditworthy, extension rent/terms are market-supported, guaranty and repair allocations are enforceable, and extended-term value exceeds sale proceeds.
decisions.tradeoffs: Can stabilize cash flow and saleability; may lock below-market rent, weak credit, or landlord capital obligations.
decisions.required: Option/notice dates, tenant financials, guaranty, market rent evidence, amendment terms, and capital plan.
decisions.verdict: Negotiate in parallel; preserve rights; sign only after credit and value tests.

decisions.when: Only if verified cash flow, reserves, insurance, and re-tenanting plan cover expiry, vacancy, capital, and tax risks better than sale/extension.
decisions.tradeoffs: Retains upside but accumulates lease-decay, vacancy, and hazard exposure; passive drift is not a strategy.
decisions.required: Funded reserve plan, downtime budget, re-tenanting strategy, insurance quotes, and exit alternatives.
decisions.verdict: Not recommended as default without a funded expiry plan.

decisions.when: Best when alternative-use or owner-user value exceeds investor NNN value after entitlement, environmental, and capital costs.
decisions.tradeoffs: Can unlock land value; entitlement, zoning, environmental, and execution risk are high.
decisions.required: Parcel zoning/overlays, Phase I/II, title, access/parking, entitlement feasibility, and buyer demand.
decisions.verdict: Test only after parcel match; no redevelopment value assumed.

decisions.when: Best when tax deferral and diversification improve after-tax wealth preservation and replacement assets are verified.
decisions.tradeoffs: Deferral is not forgiveness; timing, boot, replacement quality, and concentration risk remain.
decisions.required: Tax advisor confirmation, qualified intermediary, 45/180-day calendar, replacement underwriting, and California conformity review.
decisions.verdict: Evaluate as sale execution alternative, not a separate property verdict.

decisions.when: Only if verified debt terms improve liquidity without over-levering a short-term lease or weakening covenant resilience.
decisions.tradeoffs: Can extract liquidity but adds rate, maturity, and refinancing risk near expiry.
decisions.required: Loan documents, payoff/prepayment, rate quotes, DSCR/debt yield, lease term, and reserve capacity.
decisions.verdict: Secondary tool; not a substitute for lease/credit resolution.

decisions.when: Necessary fallback if tenant does not extend; best when downtime, capital, and replacement rent are funded and market-tested.
decisions.tradeoffs: Preserves ownership but requires capital, leasing time, and execution risk.
decisions.required: Market rent study, tenant improvement budget, leasing commissions, zoning, condition report, and reserve funding.
decisions.verdict: Build the fallback now; do not wait until expiry.

questions.question: What exactly is the asset — street address, APN, title, and vesting?
questions.obtain: Order a title commitment and ALTA survey, then match the legal description to the Assessor parcel map and ZIMAS. Do not infer a parcel from proximity to a known store.

questions.question: When does the lease actually expire, and which options, notices, and estoppels bind it?
questions.obtain: Read the executed lease and every amendment; calendar option, notice, ROFR/ROFO, assignment and estoppel deadlines. The 2030–2035 range is a premise, not a fact.

questions.question: Who decides whether the lease is renewed — the owner or the tenant?
questions.answer: Unknown for this lease. Company-wide, Jack in the Box says its real estate leases generally start with 20-year terms and carry renewal options of 1 to 20 years that are generally exercisable at its sole discretion. If this lease has such options, the tenant chooses whether to stay.
questions.obtain: Read the option clause: how many options, how long, the notice window, the rent in each option period, and whether the owner can decline. Confirm with a tenant estoppel.

questions.question: Who is legally liable for the rent — the corporate tenant, a franchisee, or a guarantor?
questions.answer: Brand identity does not answer this. At July 5, 2026 the Jack in the Box system was 149 company-operated and 1,966 franchise-operated restaurants, and the filings do not identify the obligor on any single lease. At September 28, 2025 the company leased the land or building at 1,585 of 2,136 restaurants and franchisees owned or leased 387 directly, so either arrangement is possible here.
questions.obtain: Obtain the lease counterparty, any guaranty and its scope, the franchise agreement, tenant financial statements, and a payment/default history.

questions.question: Is the tenant's credit improving or deteriorating?
questions.answer: Deteriorating on operating trend: Q3 FY2026 system same-store sales −1.1% (franchise −1.2%, company −0.9%); 2,115 restaurants, down 13 net in the quarter; the franchisee allowance for credit losses widened 70.3% to $(7,607)k; Adjusted EBITDA $61.2M.
questions.obtain: Already verified at issuer level. Re-read each quarterly release before relying on it; obligor-level credit still requires q_obligor.

questions.question: Is the tenant system's ability to pay rent rising or falling?
questions.answer: Falling on the published measures. Rent that franchisees pay the company fell 6.8% in the first 40 weeks of fiscal 2026 ($242,526 thousand against $260,254 thousand), and franchise sales per restaurant averaged $1,874 thousand in fiscal 2025 against $1,949 thousand a year earlier. These are system totals, not this restaurant.
questions.obtain: Request this restaurant's sales reports if the lease grants them, and compare its sales trend and rent-to-sales ratio with the system figures.

questions.question: Does tenant refinancing risk overlap the lease-expiry window?
questions.answer: Yes. $1,429.625M of $1,491.984M total principal (95.8%) carries anticipated repayment dates between August 2029 and February 2032, including $500.0M issued June 2026 at 7.624% with a May 2031 ARD.
questions.obtain: Already computed from the 10-Q debt note. Track each 10-Q for ARD movement and for the HoldCo and Senior ABS leverage tests that trigger the $23.3M cash sweep.

questions.question: What rent does the property collect, and what does the NNN structure still leave the owner paying?
questions.obtain: Pull base rent, escalations, percentage rent, tax/insurance/CAM recoveries, and landlord-retained items (roof, structure, parking, HVAC) from the lease; reconcile to the rent roll, operating statements, and bank deposits.

questions.question: What is the property worth today at an executable price?
questions.obtain: Commission an appraisal plus two broker opinions of value and test the market with an actual pricing exercise. Do not derive a value from citywide or county averages.

questions.question: What are the after-tax net sale proceeds?
questions.answer: The rules are known; the amount is not. California taxes individual capital gains as ordinary income with no preferential rate; a §1031 deferral requires identification within 45 days and receipt within 180 days; and the Los Angeles transfer-tax stack depends on price. Without tax basis, debt payoff, and entity structure the dollar answer stays blank.
questions.obtain: Have a tax adviser compute basis, depreciation recapture, state and federal tax, and exchange eligibility alongside a payoff statement and closing-cost estimate.

questions.question: What will a sale cost in transfer taxes alone?
questions.answer: For a City of Los Angeles property: 0.56% at or below $5,400,000 (County $0.55 + City $2.25 per $500); 4.56% from $5,400,000 to $10,900,000; 6.06% at or above $10,900,000 (ULA 4% / 5.5% on top of the base).
questions.obtain: Already computed from the published rate schedules. Confirm the City/County situs and the closing date, since the ULA thresholds reset annually with CPI.

questions.question: What does money cost if the property is held or refinanced?
questions.answer: The U.S. Treasury par curve at the November 10, 2026 close: 2Y 4.73%, 5Y 4.81%, 10Y 4.98%, 20Y 5.39%, 30Y 5.35%. The issuer’s June 2026 securitization priced at 7.624%. Neither is a property-specific loan offer or an owner discount rate; spread, LTV and terms remain unverified.
questions.obtain: Obtain term sheets from two or three lenders using the verified rent roll and property condition; price the spread, not just the index.

questions.question: Is the area's population growing or shrinking?
questions.answer: Two official series point in different directions. Census V2025: city 3,869,089 (−0.8% from the April 2020 base) and county 9,694,934 (−3.2%). DOF: city 3,806,201 (−0.9% year over year, January 1, 2026) and county 9,837,286 (−0.6%), with DOF's 2025 county level standing 158,501 (1.63%) above the Census estimate. SCAG projects county growth to 10,214,000 by 2030 against DOF's 9,727,305.
questions.obtain: Never blend agencies: pick one series and keep it. For the actual trade area, buy a radius demographic report keyed to the verified parcel and compare it with these county paths.

questions.question: Is employment growing enough to support restaurant sales?
questions.answer: Mixed but positive overall: metro nonfarm payrolls 6,282.1k (+30.2k / +0.5% year over year); county nonfarm 4,539,800 (+20,300 / +0.4%); restaurants and other eating places +7,300. Offsetting declines: information −5.7%, manufacturing −1.2%, financial activities −1.7%.
questions.obtain: Already verified. Re-read the monthly BLS/EDD releases; a turn in the leisure-and-hospitality line is the earliest warning for a restaurant tenant.

questions.question: What wage floor applies to a fast-food tenant's operating model?
questions.answer: California covered fast-food minimum wage $20.00/hour (from April 1, 2024); state general minimum wage $16.90 (January 1, 2026), rising to $17.40 on January 1, 2027; City of Los Angeles general minimum wage $18.42 (July 1, 2026).
questions.obtain: Already verified. Re-check each January and July, since a wage step that outpaces menu pricing compresses tenant coverage.

questions.answer: City median household income $81,939 and county $90,112 (2020–2024 ACS, 2024 dollars); city poverty rate 16.5%; LA-area CPI +3.7% all items and +2.8% food year over year (September 2026); October 2026 CPI-U all items +0.6% month-to-month (12-month October change not published); median gross rent $1,933/month. Trade-area income is not verified.

questions.question: What hazard loss should underwriting assume?
questions.answer: County context only: FEMA NRI composite score 100 (Very High) with expected annual loss $7.60B total and $5.95B buildings; earthquake EAL $4.57B, inland flood $2.81B, wildfire $155M; 88 federal declarations (61 fire) between 1969 and 2025; CAL FIRE maps 769,561 Very High FHSZ acres, 65.3% of mapped county acres. The parcel's FHSZ, flood zone, and fault proximity are not verified.
questions.obtain: Run official parcel-level lookups (CAL FIRE FHSZ, FEMA flood map, CGS fault-zone and liquefaction maps) once the parcel is identified, and have the insurer quote in writing.

questions.question: Can the property be insured, and at what cost?
questions.answer: Capacity is constrained: CDI reports 41,727 claims filed and $25.2B paid on the Eaton and Palisades fires, and the FAIR Plan commercial limits were raised to $20M per building and $100M per location through 2028. The subject policy, exclusions, deductibles, and premium are not verified.
questions.obtain: Obtain the current policy, loss runs, and two broker indications including a FAIR Plan fallback, then test whether full replacement cost is actually covered.

questions.question: Is earthquake risk priced into a hold?
questions.answer: USGS puts the Los Angeles region at 60% / 46% / 31% probability of M≥6.7 / 7.0 / 7.5 within 30 years (the window start date is not stated on the page); the ShakeOut M7.8 scenario totals $191B of loss, of which $87B is fire, $46B shaking, and $24B water-outage business interruption. Building retrofit status is not verified.
questions.obtain: Order a seismic and property condition assessment, confirm non-ductile or unreinforced conditions, and price retrofit capital and earthquake deductible before setting hold value.

questions.question: Is crime a trade-area obstacle?
questions.answer: Citywide 86,837 Person & Property offenses year to date (−9.2% year over year); Operations-Central Bureau 24,349 (−0.6%), or 28.0% of citywide for the same week ending November 7, 2026; larceny +13.6% and robbery +0.4%. Not unique incidents or parcel-level counts. Division-level and calls-for-service data are unverified.

questions.question: Could planned development change traffic and rent?
questions.answer: DTLA 2040 contemplates 100,000 new homes, 100,000 more work opportunities, and 175,000 additional residents through 2040; Metro's D Line Section 1 opened May 8, 2026 with Sections 2–3 forecast for 2027. Whether either touches this parcel is not verified.
questions.obtain: Check the parcel against ZIMAS and the applicable community plan, then read the specific entitlement or station-area plan rather than the citywide press release.

questions.question: Do goods-movement and trade flows matter locally?
questions.answer: Port of Los Angeles handled 10,239,318 TEUs in 2025; October 2026 was 1,026,871.65 TEUs (+21.03% year over year) and calendar-year-to-date 9,108,497.20 (+5.11%), visible on 2026-11-13 and provisional until the page confirms it. The link to a central-Los Angeles restaurant site is indirect.
questions.obtain: Already verified as context only. Use it as a regional demand signal, not as a parcel-level input.

questions.question: What decision rule should govern sell versus renew?
questions.answer: Dual-track: prepare a sale and a renewal in parallel, preserve every notice and option right, and choose only after comparing verified after-tax net sale proceeds with risk-adjusted hold value. Sell is favored when executable net proceeds exceed hold value or concentration and liquidity risk are unacceptable; renew when the obligor is creditworthy and extension terms are market-supported. Never drift to expiry without a funded re-tenanting plan.
questions.obtain: Adopt the rule now. It becomes actionable as q_identity, q_lease_dates, q_obligor, q_rent, q_value, and q_after_tax are answered.

questions.question: Which rare event would break the plan, and what trigger forces action?
questions.answer: Compound hazards dominate: a southern San Andreas rupture at ShakeOut scale, a wildfire-driven insurance withdrawal, or a tenant restructuring inside the 2029–2032 ARD window could each stop rent and impair saleability at the same time. Pre-agreed triggers: insurance non-renewal, tenant default or closure, a missed notice window, or a collapse in the buyer pool.
questions.obtain: Write the triggers into the ownership policy now, with a pre-approved action and decision owner for each, so a shock is executed rather than debated.

decision_risks.ordinary: Pricing risk as remaining term shortens; buyer financing cost; transfer taxes and income tax reduce net proceeds; reinvestment risk on the cash received.
decision_risks.severe: Removes this property's exposure to tenant failure, earthquake, fire, and insurance-market shocks from the sale date onward. A capital-market freeze before closing can delay or reprice the sale.
decision_risks.reversible: Irreversible once closed. Future rent growth and land-value upside are given up.
decision_risks.control: Verify net proceeds after transfer tax and income tax before listing; obtain more than one executable offer; decide the reinvestment plan first.

decision_risks.ordinary: Locks rent and term with one tenant; possible landlord concessions or capital obligations; rent may be set below or above market without evidence.
decision_risks.severe: Keeps full exposure to tenant or brand failure, and to earthquake, fire, flood, and insurance-availability shocks, for the extended term.
decision_risks.reversible: Partly reversible: a longer verified term can be sold later, but the extension terms themselves bind the owner.
decision_risks.control: Confirm the legal obligor and guaranty; negotiate from verified market rent; keep sale pricing in hand as the alternative; verify insurance and reserves.

decision_risks.ordinary: Value erodes as the lease term runs down; fewer buyers and lenders; vacancy and downtime at expiry if the tenant leaves.
decision_risks.severe: Highest combined exposure: a tenant shock or natural disaster close to expiry leaves no lease term, no buyer pool, and possibly no income.
decision_risks.reversible: Reversible only while time remains; each year without action narrows the sale and renewal options.
decision_risks.control: Do not hold by default. Set a dated trigger for choosing sale or renewal and fund a re-tenanting reserve.

decision_risks.ordinary: Smaller buyer pool; zoning, entitlement, and environmental diligence can lengthen or break the sale; the existing lease may block delivery.
decision_risks.severe: A planning-rule change or a discovered contamination issue can remove the land-value premium entirely.
decision_risks.reversible: Irreversible once closed; conditional contracts can fail late.
decision_risks.control: Confirm zoning and environmental status for the verified parcel before pricing; limit contingency periods; keep the investor-sale route open.

decision_risks.ordinary: 45-day identification and 180-day completion limits; any cash or non-like-kind property received is taxable; replacement property may be lower quality or over-priced under time pressure.
decision_risks.severe: A failed exchange makes the gain taxable; a market shock during the exchange window can strand proceeds or force a poor purchase.
decision_risks.reversible: Irreversible; the deferred tax carries over into the replacement property.
decision_risks.control: Engage a qualified intermediary and tax advisor before listing; pre-screen replacement property; model the fully taxable outcome as the fallback.

decision_risks.ordinary: Adds interest cost and a loan maturity; lenders size loans on remaining lease term, so proceeds shrink as expiry nears.
decision_risks.severe: Debt turns a vacancy or disaster from lost income into possible default; the loan may mature when the tenant's own refinancing dates fall due.
decision_risks.reversible: Reversible only by repayment, often with prepayment cost.
decision_risks.control: Borrow only against verified income and term; avoid a maturity inside the lease-expiry window; keep cash reserves for debt service.

decision_risks.ordinary: Downtime without rent while the owner pays taxes, insurance, and upkeep; leasing commissions, tenant improvements, and unknown market rent.
decision_risks.severe: A weak local economy or a disaster during vacancy extends downtime indefinitely; a purpose-built restaurant building may need costly conversion.
decision_risks.reversible: Reversible; ownership and future options are kept, at a carrying cost.
decision_risks.control: Budget downtime and capital before expiry; confirm permitted uses for the verified parcel; collect broker evidence on replacement tenants early.

verdicts.verdict: Keep it leased and marketable: a longer firm term with a verified, creditworthy obligor, or a replacement tenant lined up before expiry.
verdicts.reasoning: The area readings lean positive, so the location is not the weak point. The weak point is dependence on one tenant whose system readings lean negative. Secure income in an active area supports value; an approaching expiry with an uncertain tenant undermines it.
verdicts.depends_on: The executed lease, who holds the renewal options, the legal obligor, and what market rent the site would command from another tenant.

verdicts.reasoning: Wealth preservation turns on facts not yet supplied: what share of the owner's wealth this property represents, the tax basis, the need for income, and any debt. If the property is a large share of net worth, the readings favour reducing single-tenant exposure by selling or exchanging while meaningful lease term remains. If it is a small share and a vacancy could be funded, holding or renewing keeps the location's upside.
verdicts.depends_on: After-tax net sale proceeds, owner concentration and liquidity, exchange eligibility, and the renewal terms the tenant will actually sign.

verdicts.verdict: Drifting to expiry with no extension signed, no sale prepared, and no replacement tenant identified.
verdicts.reasoning: That path keeps every tenant and hazard exposure while the remaining term, and with it the sale value, runs down. It is the only path that gives up both objectives at once.
verdicts.depends_on: A dated calendar of the lease's option and notice deadlines.
